objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe the IFR rules in each class of airspace, compute time en route and total IFR fuel including the alternate, select and read the en route charts, RNAV routes, DPs, STARs and approaches for a flight, get and interpret the NOTAMs that matter, complete an FAA Form 7233-4 IFR flight plan that matches the airplane, explain the GPS and RAIM checks, recognize frost and airframe ice, explain what ice does on approach and landing and the corrective actions before takeoff, on takeoff and in cruise, find the manufacturer's icing information, and build a learner's IFR planning workflow step by step.
why: Before any IFR flight the pilot in command must become familiar with all available information, including weather, fuel requirements, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed and known ATC delays [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]. The IFH puts it plainly: the success of the flight depends largely on the thoroughness of the preflight planning [[23:317|IFH 10-26]]. If you already hold a flight instructor certificate with an airplane rating, the PTS rating table makes Area III Tasks B and C mandatory when you add the instrument instructor rating (FAA-S-8081-9E), so expect to plan and explain a real IFR flight on your test.

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner hands you a finished plan for tomorrow: GPS direct at 6,000 feet, 1+50 en route, full tanks, no alternate because "the TAF says 2,000 overcast at my arrival time," and a flight plan already filed in her app. It is February, the freezing level is 3,000 feet and the trainer is not approved for flight in icing. Before you look at a single chart, which questions would you ask her, and in what order?

key_terms.def: Class A, B, C, D and E airspace. IFR in any of it requires an IFR flight plan and an ATC clearance [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]].
The lowest published altitude between radio fixes that assures acceptable navigation signal coverage and meets obstacle clearance requirements [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]].
Meets obstacle clearance for the whole segment but assures navigation signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR; charted with an asterisk [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]].
An MEA for aircraft using GPS, charted in blue with a G suffix on Victor and colored airways and T-routes [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]] [[2:70|Chart Users' Guide p 70]].

Off-route altitude with 1,000 ft of obstruction clearance (2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas), not assessed for navigation signal, radar or communications coverage [[2:71|Chart Users' Guide p 71]].
Obstacle departure procedure: obstacle clearance by the least onerous route; may be flown without ATC clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or radar vectors [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].
Standard instrument departure: an ATC procedure, always graphic, giving obstacle clearance and a transition to the en route structure; it must be in the clearance [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].
Standard terminal arrival: an ATC coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearances and links the en route structure to the approach [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].
A NOTAM with regulatory information, such as amendments to approach procedures and charts, TFRs and GPS or WAAS status [[33:326|AIM 5-1-3]].
The GPS receiver's own integrity check; it needs 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro-aiding [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]].
A small object in the pilot's view that ices early, such as a wiper or landing light; if it ices, assume the rest of the airplane is icing [[23:90|IFH 4-13]] [[38:34|AC 91-74B 3-15b]].
Ice-contaminated tailplane stall: an iced tailplane stalls at a sufficiently negative angle of attack, most likely with flaps fully extended [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12a]].

chunks.title: The Task, and the planning sequence you will teach

body.p: The PTS asks you to describe nine elements of cross-country flight planning, from the IFR rules in each class of airspace to the icing information for the airplane on your test (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area III, Task B). The flight plan element says the plan does not have to be filed with ATC, so expect to complete one for the examiner. The Instrument lesson IR.I.C covers the pilot's side of this Task and IR.II.A covers ice protection systems; this lesson adds the instructor's side.

The IFH walks through one complete IFR flight, Birmingham to Gulfport in a Cessna 182 with a GPS approved for en route, terminal and approach use [[23:317|IFH 10-26]]. Its order is a good backbone for the workflow you teach:

What the learner does
Source
rows: All charts and materials, verified current: en route, approach, DP and STAR charts, the GPS database, the airport directory (the IFH still calls it the A/FD), nav logs and the POH/AFM
The departure and arrival airports and any preferred routing, then the approach charts, DPs and STARs
The en route charts with their minimum altitudes, then the best route and an altitude that meets the rules and the airplane's performance
An outlook briefing, with the NOTAMs and any TFRs on the route

Start it with fixes, distances, frequencies and altitudes; after a standard briefing, add POH true airspeed, power and fuel burn, weight and balance, takeoff and landing distances, and time and fuel with winds and the alternate
Complete the flight plan, get an updated briefing, compare it with personal minimums, then file
The go/no-go decision is reevaluated during the flight

callout.text: Application: teach the sequence before the details. A learner who knows where each piece fits (procedures before the route, the route before fuel, NOTAMs before the final plan) can plan a new route alone; one who memorized one app's screens cannot. The AIH bases new learning on a solid foundation of old learning, and correct habits from the start [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

check.q: A learner asks why she should study the DPs and STARs before picking her en route altitude. What do you answer?
check.a: The IFH sequence reviews the approach charts, DPs and STARs before the en route charts and the route choice [[23:319|IFH 10-28]], and a DP's climb gradient affects climb time and fuel burn [[29:44|IPH 1-28]].

chunks.title: IFR rules in each class of airspace

body.p: Start with the pilot: no one may act as pilot in command under IFR, or in weather below VFR minimums, without an instrument rating for the category and class flown or an ATP certificate [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)]]. Then the airspace: in controlled airspace no one may operate under IFR without filing an IFR flight plan and receiving an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]]. Controlled airspace is Class A, B, C, D and E, and standard IFR separation is provided to IFR aircraft in it [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].

head: Class
IFR requirements the learner should name
Source
rows: All operations IFR unless otherwise authorized; clearance before entering; two-way radio and continuous contact with ATC; transponder and ADS-B Out per 91.215 and 91.225
ATC clearance before entering; for IFR an operable VOR or TACAN receiver or an operable and suitable RNAV system; two-way radio; transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out
Two-way radio contact before entering, then maintained; transponder and ADS-B Out per 91.215 and 91.225
Two-way radio contact before entering, then maintained; if the radio fails under IFR, follow 91.185
Controlled airspace, so an IFR flight plan and a clearance
91.173 covers controlled airspace only; ATC does not separate aircraft outside controlled airspace; the 91.177 obstacle rule and the odd/even altitudes still apply

body.p: Altitudes: under IFR no one may fly below the minimum altitudes of parts 95 and 97 except for takeoff and landing; below an MEA only down to the MOCA, and when navigating by VOR only within 22 NM of that VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]. Where no minimum is published, the rule is 2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course in designated mountainous areas and 1,000 ft elsewhere [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(2)]]. In controlled airspace the learner flies the altitude ATC assigns [[60:480|14 CFR 91.179(a)]]; in uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 ft MSL it is odd thousands for magnetic courses of 0 to 179 degrees and even thousands for 180 to 359 [[60:481|14 CFR 91.179(b)]].

Equipment: IFR adds to the VFR instruments two-way radio and navigation equipment suitable for the route, a rate-of-turn indicator, a slip-skid indicator, a sensitive altimeter, a clock with seconds, an adequate generator or alternator, an attitude indicator and a heading indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. Using VOR under IFR needs a VOR check within the preceding 30 days unless the equipment is maintained under an approved procedure [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

callout.text: Controlled airspace under IFR: flight plan plus clearance [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]]. Class A: IFR only [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135]]. Class G: no clearance rule, but the altitude rules still apply [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]] [[60:481|14 CFR 91.179(b)]].

Application: have the learner trace the planned route through every class of airspace from takeoff to landing and say what rule changes at each boundary. A departure from a Class G airport under a low ceiling is the classic case: the IFH describes getting the IFR clearance by radio or telephone, with a void time or a release time [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

check.q: Your learner will depart IFR from a nontowered airport in Class G under a 600-foot overcast and says no clearance is needed until she reaches Class E. Is the regulatory part right, and what do you add?
check.a: 91.173 requires the flight plan and clearance only in controlled airspace [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]], but she still must meet the 91.177 obstacle rule and gets no ATC separation outside controlled airspace [[23:295|IFH 10-4]]. In practice she gets the clearance before takeoff, with a void or release time [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

chunks.title: Selecting and reading en route charts and RNAV routes

body.p: "Current" has a schedule: in the conterminous U.S., IFR en route charts are reissued every 56 days, and civil IFR approach charts are amended on a 56-day cycle with a change notice at the 28-day midcycle; superseded charts may contain obsolete or incomplete information [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1]]. For flight below 18,000 ft MSL the applicable chart is the en route low altitude chart, which shows airways, RNAV routes, controlled airspace limits, NAVAIDs, airports, OROCAs, reporting points, special use airspace and military training routes [[29:74|IPH 2-14]].

head: Chart item
What it means for the plan
rows: Lowest published altitude between fixes that assures navigation signal coverage and obstacle clearance across the full width of the route [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]
Obstacle clearance for the whole segment, signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR; shown only when lower than the MEA [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]
Lowest altitude at which an intersection can be determined, when that is higher than the MEA [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]
Lowest altitude to cross a fix when flying toward a higher MEA [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]
Highest altitude on the route at which signal reception is assured [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]

1,000 ft of clearance (2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas), with no signal, radar or communications assessment; for planning and contingencies [[2:71|Chart Users' Guide p 71]]
Do not file for it or accept a clearance on it [[2:70|Chart Users' Guide p 70]]

body.p: T-routes are low altitude RNAV routes for aircraft with IFR-approved GNSS, identified with a T and charted in blue [[2:70|Chart Users' Guide p 70]]. Outside Alaska, T-routes require GPS or GPS/WAAS equipment [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]]. On a joint Victor/RNAV route the GNSS and Victor MEAs are stacked in pairs, and the RNAV information is in blue [[29:76|IPH 2-16]].

Off airways, a direct route must be defined by fixes whose position can be accurately determined, and those fixes become compulsory reporting points unless ATC says otherwise [[33:334|AIM 5-1-6]]. Below 18,000 ft MSL off established airways, VOR aids that define a direct route should be no more than 80 NM apart [[33:334|AIM 5-1-6]]. Random RNAV routes are filed airport to airport and defined by waypoints, with at least one waypoint in each ARTCC area within 200 NM of the preceding center's boundary, one at each turn point, and prohibited and restricted areas avoided by 3 NM [[33:335|AIM 5-1-6]]. On direct segments outside controlled airspace and ATC surveillance the pilot is responsible for obstruction clearance, because charted MEAs apply only to the routes [[33:335|AIM 5-1-6]].

callout.text: Application: put a chart in front of the learner and have her read one segment aloud: route, course, distance, MEA, MOCA, any G value, and what each means if she loses the VOR or the GPS. Explaining is the understanding level; using it to choose the route is application [[25:65|AIH 3-14]].

check.q: Your learner asks whether the OROCA on her GPS-direct leg also guarantees she can reach ATC and receive the VORs. What do you answer?
check.a: No. OROCA gives 1,000 ft of clearance (2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas) and is not assessed for NAVAID signal, radar or communications coverage [[2:71|Chart Users' Guide p 71]] [[33:340|AIM 5-1-16]].

chunks.title: DPs and STARs: choose, check and file

body.p: There are two kinds of DP: obstacle departure procedures, printed as text or graphically, and SIDs, always graphic [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]]. An ODP gives obstacle clearance by the least onerous route and may be flown without ATC clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or radar vectors; a SID is an ATC procedure and must be in the clearance before it is flown [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]]. Part 91 pilots are strongly encouraged to file and fly a DP at night, in marginal VMC and in IMC when one is available [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]].

The design assumes the airplane crosses the departure end of the runway at least 35 ft above it, climbs to 400 ft above it before turning, and climbs at least 200 ft per NM to the minimum IFR altitude unless a higher gradient is published [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9]]. A published climb gradient is mandatory when the procedure is part of the clearance, unless increased takeoff minimums are provided and the weather allows them [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9]]. If the learner departs IFR under part 91 without filing or being cleared for an ODP, SID or DVA headings, obstacle clearance is her responsibility [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]].

Teach the conversion: the TPP rate of climb table relates climb gradients and groundspeeds, and in the IPH example 297 ft per NM at 180 knots needs 892 fpm [[29:34|IPH 1-18]]. In planning, consider how a climb gradient affects climb time and fuel burn; if the airplane cannot meet a requirement, do not file the procedure [[29:44|IPH 1-28]], and do not accept a SID whose gradient it cannot meet [[29:45|IPH 1-29]]. A pilot who does not want SIDs puts "NO SIDs" in the flight plan remarks [[29:42|IPH 1-26]].

A STAR is an ATC coded arrival route that simplifies clearances and links the en route structure to the approach [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]]. Its "expect" altitudes and speeds are planning information and not restrictions unless ATC issues them, while published speed restrictions are mandatory unless ATC changes them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]]. Using a STAR requires at least the approved chart, an RNAV STAR must be retrievable by name from the database, and a pilot who does not want STARs puts "NO STAR" in the remarks [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1]].

callout.text: "Descend via" authorizes descent at the pilot's discretion to meet the published restrictions while flying the STAR laterally; "cleared Tyler One arrival" alone clears the lateral path only, with no descent [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]] [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]].

Application: have the learner pull every DP for the expected departure runway, read the takeoff minimums and takeoff obstacle notes, and say whether the airplane, loaded as planned, can make the gradient. The AIM lists checking for an ODP, deciding whether to fly it and checking the obstacle notes as pilot responsibilities [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]].

check.q: A learner wants to file a SID that requires 450 ft per NM, but her POH shows about 500 fpm at a 100-knot climb groundspeed, which is 300 ft per NM. What do you teach?
check.a: Do not file it, and do not accept it if ATC assigns it [[29:44|IPH 1-28]] [[29:45|IPH 1-29]]. Choose another departure, or put NO SIDs in the remarks [[29:42|IPH 1-26]].

chunks.title: Selecting the approach and the alternate

body.p: Selecting the IAP starts in preflight. The IPH lists the questions: is the procedure authorized, is the weather appropriate, can the airplane perform the approach, landing or missed approach at its weight, is it properly equipped, and is the pilot qualified and current [[29:142|IPH 4-2]]. Wind and visibility can make every approach at an airport unusable, so the learner must be ready to fly other approaches than the one she planned [[29:142|IPH 4-2]]. Cold weather belongs here too: a snowflake icon with a temperature marks a Cold Temperature Airport, and at or below that temperature the pilot should calculate altitude corrections [[33:341|AIM 5-1-17]].

Then the alternate, which drives the fuel. An alternate is required unless part 97 has an approach for the first airport of intended landing and, for at least 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA, the forecast ceiling is at least 2,000 ft above the airport and the visibility at least 3 SM [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]]. An airport qualifies as the alternate if its forecast at the ETA is at or above the published alternate minimums, or, if none are published, 600-2 for a precision approach and 800-2 for a nonprecision approach; with no instrument approach, the weather must allow descent from the MEA and landing under basic VFR [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(2)]].

head: Question
Rule
Source
rows: Yes, unless an approach exists and the forecast for 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA shows at least 2,000 ft and 3 SM
Can this airport be my alternate?
Forecast at the ETA at or above its alternate minimums: published, or 600-2 precision, 800-2 nonprecision. An A NA symbol means not authorized

No. Approaches with vertical guidance are nonprecision for alternate planning

Non-WAAS GPS with FDE and a RAIM prediction: a GPS approach at the destination or the alternate, not both. WAAS: plan the LNAV or circling line with nonprecision weather

Alternate minimums are for planning only; the published landing minimums apply to the approach at the alternate

body.p: Without WAAS, unless the learner uses the FDE and RAIM prediction allowance in the table above, a required alternate must have an approach that does not need GPS, and that includes using GPS as a substitute for an out-of-service VOR at the alternate; the restriction does not apply to WAAS (TSO-C145/C146) equipment [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3]]. Mountain destinations deserve an alternate even when the forecast technically relieves the pilot of one, because some have minimums near or above the 2,000-and-3 test [[33:337|AIM 5-1-10]] [[33:338|AIM 5-1-10]].

callout.text: IPH 1-14 words the alternate rule with "and" [[29:30|IPH 1-14]]. The regulation relieves the pilot only when the ceiling and the visibility are both forecast to meet the numbers, so either one short means an alternate [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]]. The Instrument lesson IR.I.C makes the same point.

check.q: Your learner's alternate has only an RNAV (GPS) approach with an LPV line and standard alternate minimums, and her trainer has a WAAS navigator. What forecast does she need there at the ETA?
check.a: She plans the LNAV or circling line with nonprecision weather [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18]], so the standard nonprecision 800-2 applies [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]] [[29:146|IPH 4-6]].

chunks.title: Time en route and total fuel

body.p: Time is distance over groundspeed: 210 NM at 140 knots is 1.5 hours, or 1:30 [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. Fuel is flight time multiplied by the burn rate, and when there is wind the groundspeed, not the true airspeed, sets the time [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Plan for start, taxi and the higher burn in the climb, and remember that the climb groundspeed is lower than in cruise [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. The POH gives the true airspeed, cruise power and fuel burn for the forecast temperature and cruising pressure altitude, and the winds aloft turn them into time and fuel for the route and the alternate [[23:320|IFH 10-29]].

The IFR fuel rule: in IFR conditions the airplane must carry enough fuel, considering weather reports and forecasts, to fly to the first airport of intended landing, then to the alternate, then for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(3)]]. The alternate leg drops out under the same 1-2-3 test that removes the alternate requirement [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(b)]].

Worked example: 1+40 to the destination, 0+30 to the alternate and the 45-minute reserve make 2+55, about 2.92 hours. At 10 gallons per hour that is about 29.2 gallons, plus whatever the POH gives for start, taxi and climb [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)]] [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

Read the IFH log with the learner: each leg has its ETE (+16, +40, +54 and +08), the total 118 minutes is entered as 1+58, and the alternate leg is listed separately at +35 [[23:321|IFH 10-30]]. The IFH concludes that with full tanks the flight can be made nonstop with fuel for the destination, the alternate and the reserve [[23:320|IFH 10-29]].

callout.text: Check the arithmetic, even in a handbook. In the IFH log the leg distances (31, 80, 110 and 17 NM) add to 238 NM, while the total box says 228 [[23:321|IFH 10-30]]. Use it to show learners why every log gets a second look.

Application: in icing season add the AC 91-74B planning point that ice protection, drag and the extra power needed can raise fuel burn [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(8)]]. Before the approach, have the learner check that holding or stronger headwinds have not eaten into the reserve [[29:128|IPH 3-16]].

check.q: A learner computes her IFR fuel with true airspeed because "the wind averages out on a round trip." What do you say?
check.a: Each flight needs fuel to the destination, the alternate and 45 minutes [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)]]. Groundspeed sets the time, and fuel is time times burn rate, so she uses the forecast winds for this leg [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

chunks.title: NOTAMs: get them all, then read them for effect

body.p: Preflight action under 91.103 includes NOTAMs, which can affect aerodromes, runways and taxiways, obstructions, communications, airspace, NAVAID or radar status and other en route, terminal or landing information [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3]]. They are available online through FAA NOTAM Search or from Flight Service, and may be issued up to 7 days before the activity starts [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3]].

head: Type
What it carries
Source
rows: NAS NAVAIDs and public-use airports in the Chart Supplement: taxiway closures, work near runways, lighting that does not affect approach criteria; starts with a keyword such as RWY, TWY, NAV, COM, SVC or AIRSPACE
Regulatory: approach and chart amendments, TFRs, high barometric pressure, laser activity, ADS-B and FIS-B service, WAAS or GPS status, special notices
Points to other information, such as a TFR, an airshow or temporary SUA
For the centers on the route: SUA, TFRs, GPS, FDC route changes, wind turbines, UAS
ICAO format with a Q line; military NOTAMs for military and joint-use fields

body.p: What Flight Service gives matters for the briefing habit. A standard briefing includes pertinent NOTAMs, but domestic and international notices are not given unless requested, and airway, procedural and general NOTAMs (flight advisories, special security instructions, special flight rules areas) are briefed only on request [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1]].

Read for effect. A NOTAM is the primary way to learn that a NAVAID needed for the flight is out of service, even before it leaves the charts [[33:325|AIM 5-1-3]]. GPS NOTAMs use UNREL, MAY NOT BE AVBL and NOT AVBL; with UNREL the pilot must judge whether the signal is adequate and should have other navigation equipment for the route [[33:325|AIM 5-1-3]]. Site-specific WAAS MAY NOT BE AVBL NOTAMs must be requested in planning, because ATC will not advise them in flight [[33:104|AIM 1-1-18]]. In the IFH sample flight, NOTAMs put the Gulfport localizer out of service until further notice and closed a runway [[23:320|IFH 10-29]].

TFRs are issued by NOTAM [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(a)]]. In TFRs for disaster relief and for sightseeing congestion, an aircraft operating under an ATC-approved IFR flight plan is one of the listed exceptions [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)(3)]] [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(d)(2)]]. En route, the learner should get updated destination information from ATC or FSS, especially for airports without an operating tower [[33:325|AIM 5-1-3]].

callout.text: Application: after the learner reads each NOTAM aloud, ask "So what?" A NOTAM matters for its effect: which approach is gone, whether that changes the alternate, which runway is left and what that does to the landing distance.

check.q: Your learner's app showed no NOTAMs for the airways she filed, and a standard briefing from Flight Service gave none either. What might she still be missing?
check.a: Airway and procedural NOTAMs, and domestic and international notices, are given in a briefing only on request [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1]]. She should also check the ARTCC NOTAMs for the centers on her route [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3]].

chunks.title: Completing and filing the IFR flight plan

body.p: An IFR flight plan must contain the VFR flight plan items (aircraft identification, type, pilot's name and address, departure point and time, route, cruising altitude and true airspeed, first point of landing and estimated elapsed time, fuel on board in hours, persons on board) plus an alternate unless the 1-2-3 exception applies [[60:464|14 CFR 91.153(a)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(a)]]. The form is FAA Form 7233-4, the International Flight Plan; only DoD users and civilians filing stereo routes may use Form 7233-1 [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1]]. Form 7233-4 is mandatory for domestic IFR flights and for RNAV SIDs, STARs and other PBN routing [[33:332|AIM 5-1-6]].

What a single-engine IFR trainer files
Source
rows: Aircraft identification, up to seven characters
Flight rules I for IFR; type of flight is optional for a domestic flight
Aircraft type designator and wake turbulence category L (15,500 lb or less)
S for VHF radio, VOR and ILS; G for GNSS, with NAV/SBAS in Item 18 if WAAS equipped; GR with PBN/D2 for RNAV SIDs and STARs or PBN/C2 for T-routes
C for a Mode C transponder, plus the ADS-B Out code (B1 for 1090ES, U1 for UAT) with SUR/A2 in Item 18
Departure airport and time in UTC

Destination, total estimated elapsed time (HHMM) and the alternate
Remarks pertinent to ATC only, such as NO SIDs or NO STAR
Endurance, persons on board, pilot contact and aircraft color, kept by the filing service for search and rescue and not sent to ATC

body.p: Filing: file at least 30 minutes before the estimated departure time to avoid delay in getting the clearance [[33:332|AIM 5-1-6]]. ATC issues clearances based on the capabilities filed in Items 10 and 18 and expects the pilot to use what is filed [[33:332|AIM 5-1-6]]. Do not file more than one flight plan for the same flight without making sure the earlier one has been removed [[33:333|AIM 5-1-6]]. Most centers delete a flight plan that has not been activated a minimum of 2 hours after the proposed departure time [[33:339|AIM 5-1-13]]. Advise ATC if the true airspeed between reporting points varies from the filed speed by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater [[33:339|AIM 5-1-12]].

The FAA does not require the alternate to be filed in the plan sent to ATC, but the rules for establishing an alternate must still be followed; a filed alternate is not shown to controllers, so the pilot asks ATC for an amended clearance to divert [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4]].

callout.text: Old forms in an old book: the IFH still describes filing Form 7233-1, including through DUATS [[23:293|IFH 10-2]], and its sample plan is on that form [[23:322|IFH 10-31]]. Teach Form 7233-4 [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1]].

Application: the PTS says the plan does not have to be filed with ATC (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area III, Task B). For the test, complete it for the airplane you will fly and be ready to explain every Item 10 and 18 code from the equipment actually installed.

check.q: A learner's trainer has VHF radios, a VOR/ILS receiver, a WAAS GPS, a Mode C transponder and UAT ADS-B Out, and she files only G in Item 10a and C in 10b. What is missing?
check.a: Item 10a also takes S (VHF, VOR and ILS) and Item 18 NAV/SBAS for WAAS; Item 10b adds U1 with SUR/A2 in Item 18 [[34:277|AIM Appendix 4]] [[34:278|AIM Appendix 4]]. ATC clears her based on these entries [[33:332|AIM 5-1-6]].

chunks.title: GPS and RAIM: the checks before an IFR flight

body.p: RAIM is the receiver's check that the satellite signals meet the integrity needed for the phase of flight; without it the pilot has no assurance of the position's integrity [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]]. It needs at least 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro-aiding; fault detection and exclusion needs 6, or 5 plus baro-aiding, so the pilot enters the current altimeter setting as the receiver manual describes [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]]. RAIM messages come in two types: not enough satellites to check integrity, or a detected position error [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

head: Before an IFR flight with GPS, the learner checks
Source
rows: Equipment approved for IFR (TSO-C129, C196, C145 or C146) and operated per the AFM or supplement; VFR and hand-held units are not authorized for IFR
With unaugmented GPS, another approved means of navigation for the route, actively monitored when RAIM is lost
Database dates valid for the time of flight, and no provider notice limiting a waypoint or procedure
Approaches retrievable by name from the database; no manual waypoint entry for an approach
RAIM prediction when TSO-C129 equipment alone meets the RNAV requirement; a predicted continuous loss of more than 5 minutes means delay, cancel or re-route
With TSO-C145/C146 (WAAS), no prediction if WAAS coverage is confirmed along the whole route

body.p: Where to get a RAIM prediction: a manufacturer's tool, the FAA Service Availability Prediction Tool, or Flight Service, which gives RAIM information for 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA unless the pilot asks for another time [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17]]. On longer flights the learner should consider rechecking RAIM for the destination en route [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17]].

In flight: if a RAIM flag appears before the final approach waypoint, the pilot does not start the approach or descend but flies to the missed approach waypoint and goes missed; after the FAWP, climb and go missed [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17]]. The approach mode should be armed by 30 NM so the CDI changes from 5 NM to 1 NM sensitivity, and it goes active 2 NM before the FAWP, ramping to 0.3 NM [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]].

A suitable RNAV system may substitute for an out-of-service VOR, DME, NDB or compass locator, or for a missing ADF or DME, for example to hold over an out-of-service NDB [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3]]. It may not substitute for the NAVAID giving lateral guidance on the final approach segment, except on approaches with "or GPS" in the title [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3]]. If an amended chart is published, or the procedure's amendment date is on or after the database expiration date, the database must not be used for that procedure [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]].

callout.text: Application: in the airplane, have the learner show you the database dates, the RAIM or WAAS status page and the approach mode annunciation. Receivers differ even within one brand; the AIM warns against IFR use without thorough operational knowledge and notes that most receivers have a simulator mode for practice [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

check.q: A learner with a TSO-C129 GPS and no WAAS sees a predicted 8-minute RAIM gap on the T-route she filed. What are her options?
check.a: Delay, cancel or re-route to where RAIM is available [[33:341|AIM 5-1-16]], or rely on other approved navigation equipment [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. T-routes require GPS [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]], so falling back on her VOR means filing a route she can fly with it.

body.p: Structural ice forms where supercooled droplets strike and freeze, and small, narrow objects collect it fastest, which is why a protuberance in the pilot's view can serve as an "ice evidence probe" [[23:90|IFH 4-13]]. The tailplane collects ice better than the wing because it is thinner [[23:90|IFH 4-13]]. Teach the types by appearance: clear ice is glossy and transparent and can grow horns, rime is rough, milky and opaque, and mixed ice is both [[23:90|IFH 4-13]] [[23:91|IFH 4-14]].

On the ground: frost forms on a clear night when the skin cools below freezing by radiation [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4b]]. Clear ice can form on the upper wing over cold-soaked fuel even when the air is above freezing [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4b(1)]]. Even very small amounts of frost, snow or ice can hurt the wing, so all of it comes off before flight; after a heated hangar, the airplane must be dry before it goes out so the water does not refreeze [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(9)]]. Wet snow may not blow off and can hide ice beneath it [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-4b(4)]]. The AC's turbine checklists call a tactile inspection very valuable for finding clear ice, since touching the surface finds contaminants not easily seen [[38:58|AC 91-74B App 2]] [[38:59|AC 91-74B App 2]]. A strong flashlight helps at night or in low visibility [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(5)]].

In flight: expect ice in visible precipitation between +2 and -10 °C [[23:327|IFH 11-2]] and in clouds at or below 0 °C [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]]. If a wiper, landing light or other evidence probe ices, assume the rest of the airplane is icing, and near freezing look at the critical surfaces too, since they may ice first [[38:34|AC 91-74B 3-15b]]. Performance tells the story as well: drag shows as lost airspeed, or more power for the same airspeed [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-3]]. Signs of supercooled large drops include ice aft of the protected areas, granular ice or an opaque coating on side windows, ice on an unheated spinner back to the blades and ice behind nacelle inlet lips, especially with visible rain or drizzle, or drops that splatter, below +5 °C [[38:34|AC 91-74B 3-16]].

callout.text: A thin layer of rough ice on the leading edge can significantly raise the stall speed [[23:92|IFH 4-15]]. Ice that had little effect in cruise can cause a stall at a lower angle of attack and a higher speed when the learner slows for the approach [[23:91|IFH 4-14]] [[23:92|IFH 4-15]].

Application: on a frosty morning, do the preflight with the learner and have her run a hand along the wing. Then ask what she would see from the left seat in cloud: which part ices first, and where she will look.

check.q: On a sunny morning there is a thin layer of frost on top of the wing, and your learner says it will be gone by the time they taxi. What do you teach?
check.a: Even very small amounts of frost can hurt the wing, so remove all of it before flight [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(9)]], and never assume contamination will blow off on takeoff [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-4b(4)]].

chunks.title: Airframe ice in the landing phases

body.p: Most icing accidents happen in the final phases of flight, where configuration changes, low altitude, high workload and low power come together, and loss of control is often a factor [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10d]]. Ice picked up in cruise, at a moderate angle of attack, may have felt harmless; slowing down and configuring for landing can change that [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-10a]] [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7d]].

bullets: Wing stall at a higher speed: the iced wing stalls at a lower angle of attack and so a higher airspeed, and even small amounts of rough ice matter [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11a]].

Little or no stall warning: airplanes certified for icing before 2000 may give only buffet before the stall [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12b]], and in an airplane not certificated for icing the stall warning most likely will not activate before the stall [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13c]] [[38:33|AC 91-74B 3-13c]].

Tailplane stall: flap extension makes the tail's angle of attack more negative, and ICTS rarely occurs until the flaps are fully extended on susceptible airplanes [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10e]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12c]].
Drag: gear extension with ice can add excessive drag [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-10a]].
Forward visibility: windshield ice protection can be overwhelmed [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10b]].
The flare: expect lost and unpredictable lift; many icing accidents came from a stall induced in the flare [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10g]].
The rollout: higher speed means a longer landing roll, and ice on the gear can cost directional control [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11b]] [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10a]].

head: Wing stall
Tailplane stall
rows: Slowing to a high angle of attack; suspect it with any buffet if full flaps were not just set [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12b]]
Flap extension, especially full flaps, and higher speed [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12a]] [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12c]]
Buffet; abrupt roll-off from uneven ice [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11c]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11d]]
Elevator pulsing or vibration, abnormal nose-down trim change, less elevator effectiveness, sudden nose-down force or pitch [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]
Stall recovery at the first indication per the FAA template or manufacturer guidance [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11c]]
Flaps back to the previous setting with nose-up pressure, airspeed and power for that setting, slow nose-down changes, cycle boots if fitted [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]

body.p: The plan when landing with ice: unless the AFM, POH or a placard gives an icing speed, increase the approach speed by at least 25 percent for the flap setting, expect the landing distance to grow about 20 percent for each 10 percent of extra speed, and consider a reduced-flap landing in an airplane under 19,000 lb if the runway allows [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]]. Cycle boots before the approach, extend flaps in stages and, if the airplane rolls or pitches unexpectedly, return to the previous configuration as the AC's piston checklist says, though the AC adds that configuration changes then should follow the manufacturer's guidance; then carry power and limit the flare [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-10a]] [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10a]] [[38:58|AC 91-74B App 2]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10g]]. Avoid slips, limit crosswind landings and avoid tailwind landings when the stall risk is higher [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12e]].

callout.text: The recoveries pull in different directions. The IFH tailplane recovery uses nose-up elevator pressure and flap retraction and says a tailplane stall tends to worsen with more airspeed [[23:93|IFH 4-16]], while the AC's roll upset guidance lowers the pitch and keeps the flaps out unless the upper wing is clear of ice; the AC calls these in some respects opposite [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-13a]]. Teach the symptoms first, then the matching action.

check.q: On a practice approach after an unexpected encounter with light rime, your learner selects full flaps and the elevator starts pulsing as the nose drops. What is it, and what does she do?
check.a: Possible tailplane stall [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]. Retract the flaps to the previous setting with nose-up pressure, set airspeed and power for that setting, and make nose-down changes slowly [[23:93|IFH 4-16]].

chunks.title: Corrective actions: pretakeoff, takeoff and cruise

head: Phase
Corrective action
Source
rows: Plan the exits: can you climb or descend, given terrain, airspace, routes, DPs, STARs and approaches? Note airports along the route; alternates need longer runways if ice raises approach speed; carry extra fuel
Remove all frost, snow and ice; make sure no ice binds the controls, brakes or steering; check pitot heat, the pitot opening and stall warning; confirm ice protection works
Check the anti-ice and deice systems per the AFM before takeoff; brake early and gently; check full control travel and carburetor heat; defroster on high if there is no windshield protection

Verify the airspeed indicator works and pitot heat is on; expect ice further aft at the climb angle of attack; avoid climbing in autopilot vertical speed mode (highly discouraged); watch airspeed; cycle the gear only if the manufacturer recommends it

Exit by an altitude or flight path change if possible; activate boots at the first sign of ice unless the manual says otherwise; keep at least 50 to 60 percent above Vs clean; treat buffet as an imminent stall; airspeed has dropped from cruise to stall in under 3 minutes

body.p: Not approved for icing: exit as expeditiously as possible and declare an emergency, telling ATC what you are doing [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]]. The two exits are leaving the precipitation or going to an altitude above freezing, which may not be lower; if neither is available, consider an immediate landing at the nearest suitable airport [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]. In stratiform cloud a climb or descent often works, because the icing layer is often thin [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1h]].

Report the ice to ATC with the aircraft type, and request a new routing or altitude [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]. Do not accept an ATC airspeed that conflicts with the manuals or, without icing speed data, with a 50 to 60 percent margin above Vs [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b(3)]]. With the autopilot on, monitor closely for abnormal trim and attitude, and do not use vertical speed mode [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]].

callout.text: Most part 91 airplanes have no specific icing rule: 91.527 is in subpart F, which covers large and turbojet multiengine airplanes and fractional ownership aircraft [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2]]. What applies is 91.9: operate within the AFM limitations, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]].

check.q: At 7,000 ft in cloud in an airplane not approved for icing, your learner sees rime on the wing strut and 10 knots less airspeed at the same power. What should she do?
check.a: Exit as fast as she can and declare an emergency, telling ATC her plan [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]]: leave the precipitation or go to an altitude above freezing, or land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:327|IFH 11-2]], adding power to hold her airspeed margin on the way [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7b]].

body.p: AC 91-74B sends every pilot to the AFM or POH for the approved checklists and operations in icing [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-1]], and its own icing checklists supplement the AFM or POH but do not replace it [[38:57|AC 91-74B App 2]]. Operation in known icing depends on when and how the airplane was certified, and the manufacturer specifies how the installed equipment is operated [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-12e]].

bullets: Certificated if the AFM or POH references part 25 appendix C icing conditions, or 14 CFR 23.1419 at Amendment 23-14 or later [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12c]].
Or if the TCDS certification basis references 23.1419 at Amendment 23-14 or higher, or SFAR 23 [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12c]].
If the AFM or POH has only a minimum equipment list for icing, the basis is before Amendment 23-14 (1973) [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12c]].
Supplemental Type Certificate items may affect the icing certification [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12b]].

body.p: What to find in the manual, and teach the learner to find: the procedures for the ice protection systems and any airspeed minimums during or after icing [[23:94|IFH 4-17]]; icing approach speeds and any flap limit, which usually exists because of ICTS susceptibility [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]] [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12d]]; limits on flap use in icing, which many AFMs restrict for extended periods [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-9d]]; autopilot use in icing [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]]; approved deicing fluids [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-4b(3)]]; whether the ice detector is advisory or primary [[38:33|AC 91-74B 3-15a]]; and aircraft-specific cues for supercooled large drops [[23:94|IFH 4-17]].

Stall warning follows the certification basis: at Amendment 23-43 or higher the stall warning works in the certified icing conditions, and below it the pilot should not rely on it in icing [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-12d]]. Before 1973 part 23 airplanes had no icing test requirements, and their ice protection should be seen as a means to help exit icing [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-12d]]. Ice protection on an airplane not certificated for icing is for emergency use only [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13c]].

callout.text: Application: K9 is about the airplane on your test. Bring its POH with the icing pages tabbed: the limitation or placard on flight into known icing, the ice protection procedures and any icing speeds. Then explain them to the examiner as you would to a learner.

check.q: A learner flies a single that is not certificated for icing but has heated pitot and an alternate static source. She asks whether that makes light icing acceptable. What do you answer?
check.a: No. Nearly all aircraft have pitot heat and alternate static [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13a]]; in an airplane not certificated for icing she must avoid icing and exit at once if she meets it [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13b]], within the AFM limitations and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]].

chunks.title: Teaching the workflow: from your demonstration to her plan

body.p: Plan the teaching in building blocks: correct habits from the start, and new learning on a solid base of old learning [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Use the demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance, instructor supervision and evaluation [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Application: in IFR planning that means (1) the rules and charts on the ground, (2) one complete plan you demonstrate aloud, (3) the learner plans while you supervise, (4) she plans a scenario flight alone and briefs you, and (5) the plan meets a change.

For a scenario flight, the instructor and learner set the destination, the desired outcome, the desired level of performance and possible in-flight changes, and the learner plans the route, destinations, weather, NOTAMs and possible emergency procedures [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. Hand the planning to the learner as early as possible and move to the mentor role [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. Have her make the weather go/no-go call before each flight [[25:32|AIH 1-28]], and review the 5 Ps (plan, plane, pilot, passengers, programming) at the decision points, starting in the planning room [[25:20|AIH 1-16]] [[25:22|AIH 1-18]].

head: Learning level
What it looks like in IFR planning
rows: Recites 1-2-3 and 600-2/800-2 without being able to use them [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Explains why an LPV approach counts as nonprecision for alternate planning [[25:65|AIH 3-14]] [[29:146|IPH 4-6]]
Determines the alternate, the fuel and the Item 10 codes for a real flight [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Sees that one NOTAM changes the approach, the alternate and the fuel together [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]

callout.text: Application: errors to watch for (instructor experience, not a source list): fuel computed with true airspeed, an alternate checked only at the ETA instead of 1 hour either side, a MOCA used beyond 22 NM of the VOR, a SID filed that the airplane cannot climb, Item 10 copied from an old plan, NOTAMs read but not applied, and no icing exit. Name the error, show the source and have the learner fix her own plan.

How the examiner tests it: expect to describe each element and complete a flight plan that matches the proposed flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area III, Task B). The evaluator assesses risk management with scenarios that combine Tasks, such as weather decisions and performance planning (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

check.q: Your learner recites every alternate rule perfectly, but when the destination forecast drops to 1,500 broken an hour after her ETA she still plans no alternate. Which learning level is she at, and what do you do?
check.a: Rote: she can repeat the rule but not use it [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. Give her scenario flights where the forecast or a NOTAM changes the plan, and let her make the decisions [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

scenario.title: A February plan with a new instrument learner
scenario.setup: Your instrument learner, about 30 hours into training, has planned an IFR flight of about 180 NM in your club's fixed-gear single. It has a WAAS GPS navigator, one VOR/ILS receiver, a Mode C transponder and UAT ADS-B Out, and it is not certificated for flight in icing. The destination is a nontowered airport with an RNAV (GPS) approach and a VOR approach. It is February: tops are forecast at 8,000 ft and the freezing level at 3,000 ft along the route. She planned alone, and you are reviewing the plan with her the evening before.

questions.q: Her NOTAM printout shows a GPS testing NOTAM (MAY NOT BE AVBL) covering the destination area at her ETA. What does it change?
questions.a: During testing, GPS and WAAS may not be available, and ATC will tell pilots asking for a GPS approach and ask their intentions [[33:325|AIM 5-1-3]] [[33:104|AIM 1-1-18]]. A sound plan treats GPS as unavailable for that time: the VOR approach becomes the plan, so she checks that VOR's NOTAMs [[33:325|AIM 5-1-3]] and picks an alternate she can reach and fly without GPS.

questions.q: She filed G in Item 10a and C in Item 10b. What do you have her change, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Add S for the VHF radio, VOR and ILS, NAV/SBAS in Item 18 for WAAS, and U1 in Item 10b with SUR/A2 in Item 18 [[34:277|AIM Appendix 4]] [[34:278|AIM Appendix 4]]. ATC issues clearances based on the capabilities filed [[33:332|AIM 5-1-6]].

questions.q: She planned 6,000 ft on an airway with a 4,000-ft MEA to stay "out of the bumps." What do you discuss?
questions.a: At 6,000 she would be in cloud above a 3,000-ft freezing level. An airplane not certificated for icing must avoid icing [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13b]], and the exit plan is made in preflight from the minimum altitudes [[38:45|AC 91-74B 5-4a(3)]]. With the MEA above the freezing level, there is no descent to above-freezing air at or above the MEA on that airway. Her planning has to emphasize ice avoidance and an alternative course of action [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1m]]; if she cannot find one, not going is the honest answer.

questions.q: She asks you to just tell her whether to go. What do you do?
questions.a: Have her make the go/no-go call and explain it, then discuss it; the final choice to fly on a training flight stays with you [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Turning planning over to her early and acting as mentor is how the AIH builds judgment [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

questions.q: Two days later the freezing level is forecast at 6,000 ft with tops at 5,000 ft, and she goes. The airplane has frost on it. What do you hold her to before taxi?
questions.a: Remove all frost, snow and ice [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(9)]], check that nothing binds the controls, brakes or steering, check the pitot heat, pitot opening and stall warning, and do not assume anything will blow off [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-4b(4)]].

questions.q: After the flight, how do you debrief her planning?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then your assessment, compared in discussion [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Grade her risk management as explain, practice or manage/decide, aiming for decisions she makes without your help [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

skills.do: Complete FAA Form 7233-4 for the airplane you will use on the practical test and explain each entry as you would to a learner: Items 7 to 19, the Item 10 and 18 codes from the installed equipment, the route in filing format, the alternate and the remarks.
skills.practice: Build the plan for one real route and check every code against AIM Appendix 4 [[34:277|AIM Appendix 4]] [[34:278|AIM Appendix 4]] [[34:287|AIM Appendix 4]]; then have a classmate play the examiner and ask why for each box.

skills.do: Talk a learner through a complete IFR plan in the IFH order: charts and currency, procedures, route and altitude, briefing and NOTAMs, time and fuel with the alternate, GPS checks, an icing exit, and the flight plan, ending with a go/no-go decision she makes.
skills.practice: Use the IFH sample flight as the model [[23:319|IFH 10-28]] [[23:320|IFH 10-29]], then plan a real route in your test airplane and brief it aloud in the demonstration-performance order [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

quiz.q: Your learner will fly IFR from a nontowered airport in Class G and climb into Class E at 700 ft AGL. Which statement about the rules is correct?
options: No clearance is needed anywhere if she stays below 18,000 ft
She needs a filed flight plan and a clearance for IFR in Class E
She needs a clearance only for any Class B or C on her route
She needs a clearance before IFR flight in every class of airspace
quiz.why: IFR in controlled airspace requires a filed IFR flight plan and an ATC clearance [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]], and Class E is controlled airspace [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]]. Class G is uncontrolled, so the last option overstates the rule; there the 91.177 altitude rule still applies [[33:189|AIM 3-3-3]].

quiz.q: On a Victor airway with an MEA of 6,000 and a MOCA of *4,800, your learner, navigating by VOR, wants 5,000 ft to stay below the ice, and ATC will assign it. When does 91.177 allow it?
options: Anywhere on the segment, since the MOCA covers its full length
Only while she is in radar contact with the center
Never; a MOCA is an emergency figure, not an altitude
Only within 22 NM of the VOR she is navigating by
quiz.why: Below the MEA down to the MOCA is allowed with the navigation signals available, and when navigating by VOR only within 22 NM of it [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]. The MOCA gives obstacle clearance for the whole segment but signal coverage only within 22 NM [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]], so the first option forgets the signal part.

quiz.q: Your learner departs IFR under part 91 from a runway with a published ODP, and her clearance names no SID or vectors. What does the AIM say about the ODP?
options: She may fly it without a specific ATC clearance
She must not fly it unless ATC names it in the clearance
It applies only to airplanes with more than two engines
It may be flown only from an airport with a tower
quiz.why: ODPs are recommended for obstruction clearance and may be flown without ATC clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or radar vectors; a SID is the one that needs a clearance [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]]. If she departs without filing or being cleared for a DP, obstacle clearance is her own responsibility [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9]]. ODPs are published for nontowered airports too [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]].

quiz.q: The figure shows the IPH rate of climb example. A departure requires 297 ft per NM and the climb groundspeed will be 180 knots. What climb rate is needed?
options: About 297 fpm, the same as the gradient
About 535 fpm
About 892 fpm at that groundspeed
About 1,070 fpm at that speed
quiz.why: The TPP rate of climb table relates the gradient to groundspeed, and the IPH example of 297 ft/NM at 180 knots needs 892 fpm [[29:34|IPH 1-18]]. The arithmetic agrees: 180 knots is 3 NM per minute, and 3 times 297 is about 891.

quiz.q: ATC says "Cleared Tyler One arrival." Your learner asks whether she may start down to the expect altitude printed on the STAR. What do you tell her?
options: Yes; expect altitudes on a STAR are mandatory crossing restrictions
No; that is a lateral clearance, and expect altitudes are for planning
Yes; every STAR clearance includes a descend via authorization
No; she must cancel the STAR before she may leave her altitude
quiz.why: That clearance authorizes the lateral path only, with no descent [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]], and expect altitudes are not restrictions unless ATC issues them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]]. A "descend via" clearance is what would authorize the descent [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].

quiz.q: The destination TAF shows BKN025 and 5 SM at the ETA, but an FM group 45 minutes after the ETA brings BKN018. Your learner plans no alternate. What do you say?
options: That is fine; only the forecast at the ETA itself counts
That is fine; 1,800 ft is above the 800-2 nonprecision minimum
She needs one only if the visibility also drops below 3 SM
She needs one; 2,000 ft must hold until 1 hour after the ETA
quiz.why: To skip the alternate, the forecast must show at least a 2,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]]; either one short requires an alternate. The 800-2 figure is the test for an alternate airport, not the destination [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: In IFR conditions with an alternate required, the ETE to the destination is 1+30 and the alternate is 0+25 beyond. What flight time must the fuel cover under 91.167?
options: 1+55, the two legs with no reserve
2+25, adding the 30-minute VFR day reserve
2+40, adding 45 minutes at normal cruising speed
3+25, adding a 45-minute reserve after each leg
quiz.why: 91.167 requires fuel to the first airport of intended landing, then to the alternate, then 45 minutes at normal cruising speed [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(3)]]: 1+30 plus 0+25 plus 0+45 is 2+40. The 30-minute reserve is the VFR day rule [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]].

quiz.q: Your learner calls Flight Service for a standard briefing. Which NOTAMs does the AIM say she gets only if she asks for them?
options: Pertinent NOTAMs for her departure and destination airports
Airway and procedural NOTAMs, and domestic notices
TFRs only; the briefer gives everything else automatically
None; the briefer must give every NOTAM on the route
quiz.why: FSS must give pertinent NOTAMs in a standard briefing, but domestic and international notices, and airway, procedural and general NOTAMs, are given only on request [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1]]. So the first option is given anyway, and the last one overstates the briefer's duty.

quiz.q: A trainer has VHF radios, a VOR/ILS receiver, a WAAS GPS, a Mode C transponder and 1090ES ADS-B Out. Which Item 10 entries fit it?
options: 10a S and G, NAV/SBAS; 10b C and B1, SUR/A2
10a G only; 10b N, since ADS-B is not filed in the U.S.
10a S only; 10b C, since GPS goes in the remarks
10a SGB with PBN/D2; 10b E with SUR/A2
quiz.why: S covers VHF radio, VOR and ILS, and G shows GNSS with NAV/SBAS in Item 18 when WAAS equipped [[34:277|AIM Appendix 4]]. Item 10b takes C for Mode C and B1 for 1090ES Out, with SUR/A2 in Item 18 [[34:278|AIM Appendix 4]]. E is a Mode S code, and a PBN/ code goes with R in Item 10a [[34:273|AIM Appendix 4]].

quiz.q: Your learner's TSO-C129 GPS (no WAAS) is her only RNAV system for a T-route, and the prediction shows an 8-minute continuous RAIM loss on it. What does the AIM call for?
options: Delay, cancel or re-route to where RAIM is available
Continue; only gaps over 10 minutes matter en route
Continue; the receiver will warn her if the position degrades
Continue, and fly that segment by dead reckoning
quiz.why: When TSO-C129 equipment alone meets the RNAV requirement, a predicted continuous RAIM loss of more than 5 minutes on any part of the flight means delay, cancel or re-route [[33:340|AIM 5-1-16]] [[33:341|AIM 5-1-16]]. The AIM requires a plan for a predicted loss of RAIM (other approved navigation, re-route, delay or cancel), so waiting for the receiver's in-flight alert is not one of the options [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

quiz.q: After a long flight at altitude in subfreezing air, the airplane sits on the ramp in drizzle at +4 °C. Your learner finds a thin, nearly invisible layer on top of the wing over the fuel tanks. What is the likely cause, and the action?
options: Dew that will evaporate during the takeoff roll
Frost that is harmless once the sun is up
Rime that is acceptable if thinner than 1/8 inch
Clear ice from cold-soaked fuel; remove it
quiz.why: After prolonged flight at altitude, clear ice can form on upper wing surfaces over cold-soaked fuel when moisture meets the cold wing, even with the air above freezing [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4b(1)]]. All frost, snow and ice must come off, since even small amounts hurt the wing, and no contamination should be assumed to blow off [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(9)]] [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-4b(4)]].

quiz.q: After an unplanned ice encounter, your learner's POH gives no icing approach speed. Her normal approach speed is 70 knots. What does AC 91-74B recommend?
options: Nothing extra; more speed risks a tailplane stall
At least 10 percent more, about 77 knots
Half the gust factor added, about 75 knots
At least 25 percent more, about 88 knots
quiz.why: Unless the AFM, POH or a placard gives an icing speed, increase approach speed by at least 25 percent for the flap setting [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]]: 70 times 1.25 is 87.5 knots. Higher speed does move a susceptible airplane toward tailplane stall, which is why the AFM's own limits come first [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12c]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner plans IFR into a Class B primary airport with a WAAS GPS and an inoperative VOR receiver. Does 91.131 allow it?
options: No; IFR in Class B requires an operable VOR or TACAN
Yes, but only on a T-route all the way to the airport
No; Class B requires dual navigation receivers for IFR
Yes; an operable, suitable RNAV system meets the rule
final_quiz.why: For IFR in Class B the airplane needs an operable VOR or TACAN receiver or an operable and suitable RNAV system [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(c)]], plus two-way radio, a transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(d)]].

final_quiz.q: In uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 ft MSL your learner flies IFR on a magnetic course of 200 degrees. Which cruising altitudes does 91.179 give her?
options: Odd thousands, such as 5,000 or 7,000
Even thousands, such as 4,000 or 6,000
Even thousands plus 500, like 4,500
Any altitude at or above the OROCA
final_quiz.why: In uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 ft MSL, IFR courses of 180 to 359 degrees use even thousands [[60:481|14 CFR 91.179(b)]]. Thousands plus 500 is the VFR rule [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner plans a GPS-direct leg off airways and wants to treat the OROCA like an MEA. What is true of the OROCA?
options: It assures VOR reception and radar coverage in the quadrant
It is the legal MEA for any direct route across the quadrant
It gives 500 ft of clearance above the highest obstacle
It gives obstacle clearance, with no signal or radar check
final_quiz.why: OROCA gives 1,000 ft of clearance (2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas) and is not assessed for NAVAID signal, radar or communications coverage [[2:71|Chart Users' Guide p 71]] [[33:340|AIM 5-1-16]].

final_quiz.q: In the lower panel of the figure, the segment from TOMMY to YATES shows 10000, 7000G and *6700. Your learner navigates by GPS on the joint route. Which MEA applies to her on that segment?
options: 10,000 ft, the Victor MEA for every airplane
7,000 ft, the GNSS MEA with the G suffix
6,700 ft, the asterisked value, on the whole segment
6,700 ft, but only within 22 NM of TOMMY
final_quiz.why: GNSS MEAs carry a G suffix and are charted in blue, and on joint routes the GNSS and Victor MEAs are stacked in pairs [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]] [[29:76|IPH 2-16]]. The asterisked 6,700 is a MOCA, not an MEA, which assures signal coverage only within 22 NM of a VOR [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]]; TOMMY is not a VOR.

final_quiz.q: A SID requires 400 ft per NM to 3,000 ft, and your learner's climb groundspeed will be 90 knots. What rate of climb does she need?
options: About 400 fpm
About 450 fpm
About 600 fpm
About 800 fpm
final_quiz.why: 90 knots is 1.5 NM per minute, so 400 ft per NM times 1.5 is 600 fpm; the TPP rate of climb table does this conversion [[29:34|IPH 1-18]]. The gradient is mandatory when the procedure is part of her clearance [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner does not want the RNAV STAR into her destination. How should she tell ATC?
options: Write NO STAR in the flight plan remarks
File it, then refuse it on first contact
Leave Item 10a blank so it cannot be assigned
Nothing; STARs are never assigned to pistons
final_quiz.why: A pilot who does not want a STAR puts NO STAR in the remarks, or less desirably tells ATC [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1]]. ATC may assign a STAR whenever it deems appropriate, so the last option is wrong [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1]]. For RNAV procedures the AIM also gives an Item 18 entry, NAV/RNV A0 and/or D0 [[33:334|AIM 5-1-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner has a TSO-C129 GPS with FDE and will do a RAIM prediction. Her destination's only approach is RNAV (GPS). May her required alternate also be an airport with only an RNAV (GPS) approach?
options: Yes, if it forecasts 800-2 at the ETA
No; a GPS approach at one of the two, not both
Yes, if she plans the LPV line there
No; non-WAAS GPS is never used for an alternate
final_quiz.why: Non-WAAS GPS users with FDE who do a RAIM prediction may file based on a GPS approach at the destination or the alternate, but not both [[33:95|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3]]. LPV is a WAAS capability [[34:279|AIM Appendix 4]], and the last option ignores the one-airport allowance.

final_quiz.q: Your learner's alternate has an ILS and an RNAV (GPS) with LPV, both with standard alternate minimums. She plans on the ILS. What forecast does she need there at the ETA?
options: 600 ft and 2 SM, the precision standard
800 ft and 2 SM, the nonprecision standard
2,000 ft and 3 SM, the destination test
Her ILS landing minimums plus 200 ft
final_quiz.why: With standard alternate minimums an airport qualifies on a forecast of 600-2 for a precision approach [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]]. Had she planned on the LPV, 800-2 would apply, since approaches with vertical guidance count as nonprecision here [[29:146|IPH 4-6]].

final_quiz.q: A NOTAM for an area on your learner's route reads GPS UNREL. What does the AIM say that means for her?
options: GPS is switched off there, and GPS approaches are banned
Service may not be available; she judges it and has backup
Only WAAS vertical guidance is affected; lateral is fine
It is for military users only; civil GPS is unaffected
final_quiz.why: UNREL means the expected level of GPS and WAAS service may not be available; the pilot must decide whether the signal is adequate, and aircraft should have other navigation equipment for the route [[33:325|AIM 5-1-3]].

final_quiz.q: A NOTAM raises the MDA on the approach your learner plans at her destination. Which kind of NOTAM is it, and what does she do?
options: NOTAM (D); she flies the chart, since charts outrank NOTAMs
Pointer NOTAM; it only points to the next chart edition
Military NOTAM; it applies only at joint-use airports
FDC NOTAM; it amends the procedure, so she plans with it
final_quiz.why: Amendments to published IAPs and other current charts are FDC NOTAMs, which carry regulatory information [[33:326|AIM 5-1-3]]. A NOTAM is cancelled only when the information is published on the chart or the condition returns to normal [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3]], so the chart does not outrank it.

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks whether the controller will see the alternate she enters on her flight plan. What does the AIM say?
options: Yes; controllers use it to plan her lost-comms route
Yes; after a missed approach ATC clears her there automatically
No; it is accepted but not shown, so she must ask to divert
No; the filing service keeps it with Item 19 for search only
final_quiz.why: Alternate information is accepted by the computer but not presented to controllers; to divert, the pilot notifies ATC and requests an amended clearance [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4]]. The rules for having an alternate still apply [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner filed an IFR plan in one app, then decides to file the same flight in a second app. What does the AIM say?
options: Fine; ATC keeps the newest plan and drops the old one
Fine, if both are filed 30 minutes before departure
Remove the first plan before filing another for that flight
Only Flight Service may take a second plan for one flight
final_quiz.why: Pilots must not file more than one flight plan for the same flight without making sure the earlier one has been removed, because multiple versions can lead to unsafe conditions and errors [[33:333|AIM 5-1-6]].

final_quiz.q: In cloud at -4 °C, ice appears on your learner's wing strut, but she cannot see any on the wing. What does the AC say she should assume?
options: The rest of the airplane, tail included, is also icing
The wing is clean, since struts ice and wings stay clear
It is only frost from the cold strut and will sublimate
The strut ice will shed by itself once she adds power
final_quiz.why: If ice builds on an ice evidence probe, assume the rest of the aircraft is also accumulating ice [[38:34|AC 91-74B 3-15b]]. Small objects ice first, and the tailplane collects ice better than the wing [[23:90|IFH 4-13]].

final_quiz.q: On short final with ice on the airplane, your learner plans a normal idle-power flare. What does AC 91-74B recommend instead?
options: Flare higher and longer to bleed off the extra speed
Select full flaps late to shorten the landing roll
Carry higher-than-normal power and limit the flare
Slip to lose height so the speed can stay normal
final_quiz.why: With ice on the leading edges expect lost and unpredictable lift in the flare; carry higher-than-normal power and limit the flare, since many icing accidents came from a stall induced in the flare [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10g]]. Slips should be avoided when the stall risk is higher [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12e]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing through a cloud layer near freezing, your learner uses the autopilot in vertical speed mode. What hazard does the AC name?
options: As ice cuts climb performance, the rate is held until a stall
The autopilot cannot stay engaged while pitot heat is on
Vertical speed mode burns into the 45-minute fuel reserve
Vertical speed mode makes ice form only on the tail
final_quiz.why: Ice accretion reduces climb performance, and if the vertical speed is not reduced the autopilot will hold the rate until stall; climbing in VS mode in icing is highly discouraged, so monitor airspeed [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6c]] [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6d]].

final_quiz.q: A POH for an airplane approved for flight into known icing limits flaps to 10 degrees in icing. Why is a limit like that most likely there?
options: Flaps beyond 10 burn too much fuel with ice on
The stall warning fails beyond 10 degrees of flap
Tailplane stall susceptibility with more flap
The boots cannot inflate with the flaps lowered
final_quiz.why: When an AFM has a maximum flap limitation in icing, it is usually because of ICTS susceptibility [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12d]]. On airplanes certified for icing after 1994, following the AFM limitations and procedures precludes ICTS [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12c]].

takeaways: Controlled airspace under IFR means a flight plan and a clearance; Class G still has the altitude rules.
Time is distance over groundspeed; IFR fuel is to the destination, then the alternate, then 45 minutes.
No alternate only if the destination has an approach and 2,000 and 3 hold from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA; alternate minimums are for planning, and APV counts as nonprecision.
Read charts and procedures for what they demand: MEA, MOCA or GNSS MEA, a gradient the airplane can make, expect or mandatory.
NOTAMs matter for their effect; ask for the ones Flight Service gives only on request.
File Form 7233-4 codes that match the installed equipment; ATC clears you on what you file.
GPS: approved receiver, current database, NOTAMs, and a RAIM prediction unless WAAS coverage is confirmed.
Ice: remove all of it, plan the exits before takeoff, and on landing add speed and limit flaps and flare per the AFM.
cfi_notes: IFH Chapter 10 is dated: it names DUATS, the A/FD and FAA Form 7233-1 [[23:293|IFH 10-2]]. The current AIM says civil domestic IFR flights use Form 7233-4, and only DoD users and stereo-route filers may use 7233-1 [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1]].

91.169(a) says an IFR flight plan must include an alternate unless the 1-2-3 exception applies [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(a)]], while AIM Appendix 4 says the FAA does not require the alternate in the plan sent to ATC, though the rules for establishing one must be followed [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4]]. Teach learners to meet the rule and enter the alternate; the AIM adds that it helps search and rescue [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4]].

STAR MEAs: the IPH says MEAs printed on STARs are not valid unless stated in a clearance or for lost communications [[29:128|IPH 3-16]]; the AIM says MEAs are not restrictions but pilots must remain above all MEAs unless ATC instructs otherwise [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]]. Teach the AIM.
IPH 1-14 words the alternate rule with "and" [[29:30|IPH 1-14]]; the regulation relieves the pilot only when both the ceiling and the visibility meet the numbers [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]].

Tailplane stall and flaps: the IFH says an iced tail may stall after full or partial flap deployment [[23:92|IFH 4-15]]; AC 91-74B says there are no known ICTS incidents with partial flaps and it rarely occurs until the flaps are fully extended [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12a]] [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10e]]. Teach full flaps as the high-risk point, and watch every flap change.

Icing intensity: the IFH 11-2 list says light icing is no problem with equipment on [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]; AC 91-74B tells pilots to consider exiting even trace and light icing [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-2]]. Teach the AC, and remember that most trainers are not certificated for icing at all.

The IFH sample log has arithmetic problems: the legs add to 238 NM against a 228 NM total, and the alternate leg's 18 gallons in 35 minutes is a far higher burn than the other legs [[23:321|IFH 10-30]]. Use it for the layout and let learners find the errors.

AC 91-74B (2015) still names Flight Watch, TWEB and the Airport/Facility Directory [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-3]] [[38:45|AC 91-74B 5-3]]. Use it for icing technique, and the AIM for current services and planning.

How it is tested: for a holder of a flight instructor certificate with an airplane rating, Tasks B and C of Area III are mandatory when adding the instrument instructor rating (FAA-S-8081-9E, rating table). Expect to plan a real flight in the test airplane, complete the flight plan without filing it, and explain the airplane's own icing information (Task B, elements 5 and 9).
gaps: The TPP, the Chart Supplement and real en route charts are not among the sources; chart symbols and procedures are taught from the AIM, IPH and Chart Users' Guide, so practice with current published charts.
True airspeed, fuel flow, climb performance, start-taxi-climb fuel, weight and balance and landing distances for the training airplane come from its POH, not these sources.
No source here gives a specific trainer's GPS receiver class (TSO-C129, C145 or C146) or its icing limitations; both are in its AFM and supplements.
Ground deicing fluids and holdover times for small airplanes (AC 135-17) are not in these sources.
No source gives a common-errors list for IFR cross-country planning; the errors named in this lesson are instructor experience and are labeled as application.
No source here states outright that IFR in Class G needs no clearance; the lesson teaches it from the 91.173 wording, which limits the flight plan and clearance requirement to controlled airspace.

activities.title: Work the numbers: time, fuel, climb and ice
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A leg of 80 NM at a 120-knot groundspeed. How many minutes?
items.why: Time = distance / groundspeed: 80 / 120 = 0.667 hour = 40 minutes [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. The IFH log shows +40 for its 80-NM Kewanee leg at 120 knots [[23:321|IFH 10-30]].

items.q: IFR with an alternate required: 1+45 to the destination, 0+30 to the alternate, 10 GPH, and the POH says 2 gallons for start, taxi and climb. Minimum gallons at engine start?
48 gallons usable at 12 GPH, and the alternate is 0+40 beyond the destination. Ignoring taxi and climb, what is the longest time to the destination, in minutes, that still meets 91.167?
items.why: Endurance 48 / 12 = 4 hours = 240 minutes. Take off 40 for the alternate and 45 for the reserve: 240 - 85 = 155 minutes, or 2+35 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(3)]].

items.q: A SID requires 350 ft per NM and the climb groundspeed will be 120 knots. What climb rate is needed?
items.why: 120 knots is 2 NM per minute; 350 x 2 = 700 fpm. The TPP rate of climb table makes the same conversion [[29:34|IPH 1-18]].

items.q: Normal approach speed 72 knots, and the POH gives no icing speed. Minimum approach speed with ice on the airplane, per AC 91-74B?
items.why: At least 25 percent above the non-icing speed for the flap setting: 72 x 1.25 = 90 knots [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]].

items.q: Normal landing distance 1,500 ft. The approach is flown 10 percent faster because of ice. Estimated landing distance?
items.why: Estimate 20 percent more landing distance for each 10 percent more airspeed: 1,500 x 1.2 = 1,800 ft, more if the runway is contaminated [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10f]].

items.q: Clean stall speed 55 knots and no icing speed in the manual. The minimum cruise margin in icing at 1.5 Vs is how many knots?
items.why: AC 91-74B recommends at least 50 to 60 percent above Vs in a clean configuration (Vs x 1.5 or 1.6): 55 x 1.5 = 82.5 knots [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]].

activities.title: True or false: GPS and RAIM
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: RAIM needs at least five satellites, or four plus baro-aiding.
A hand-held GPS may be used for IFR navigation if its database is current.
cards.why: False. VFR and hand-held GPS systems are not authorized for IFR navigation or approaches [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

cards.s: With a WAAS receiver, no RAIM prediction is needed if WAAS coverage is confirmed along the whole route.
If a RAIM flag appears before the final approach waypoint, the pilot may continue down to the MDA.
cards.why: False. Do not start the approach or descend; fly to the missed approach waypoint and go missed [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17]].

cards.s: An approach may be flown from waypoints typed in by latitude and longitude if they match the chart.
cards.why: False. The approach must be retrieved by name from the database; manual entry is not permitted [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

cards.s: Flight Service gives RAIM information for 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA unless asked for another time.

activities.title: Coaching a February IFR plan, one call at a time
activities.intro: Your instrument learner is planning tomorrow's IFR flight in a single that is not approved for icing and has a WAAS GPS. You coach; she decides.

steps.s: The airway's MEA is 6,000 ft, the freezing level 4,000 ft and the tops 7,000 ft. She plans 6,000 ft. What do you ask first?
options: Nothing; 6,000 ft meets the MEA, so the plan is legal
What her exit is if ice forms, given the MEA and the freezing level
Whether she could file 8,000 ft to be on top the whole way
Whether the autopilot can hold altitude in the clouds
steps.why: Icing exit strategies are set in preflight, including whether climbing or descending works with the required altitudes [[38:45|AC 91-74B 5-4a(3)]] [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(3)]]. Asking, not telling, keeps the decision hers [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

steps.s: She re-plans a lower route with a 3,000-ft MEA, below the freezing level. The destination forecast is OVC015 from 1 hour before to 1 hour after her ETA, and she plans no alternate because the approach minimums are 400 ft. What do you say?
options: Fine; the approach minimums decide the alternate
Fine, as long as she carries 45 minutes of extra fuel
She needs an alternate only if visibility is also under 3 SM
She needs an alternate; the ceiling is forecast under 2,000 ft
steps.why: No alternate is needed only if the forecast shows at least 2,000 ft and 3 SM from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]].

steps.s: Her alternate has only an RNAV (GPS) approach with standard alternate minimums. She plans the LPV line there because her navigator has WAAS. What do you correct?
options: Plan the LNAV or circling line with nonprecision weather, 800-2
Nothing; WAAS lets her plan the LPV line at an alternate
She may not plan any GPS approach at an alternate airport
Plan the LPV line but add 200 ft and 1/2 mile to it
steps.why: WAAS users plan the LNAV or circling line at an alternate with the part 91 nonprecision weather [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18]], which is 800-2 with standard alternate minimums [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]].

steps.s: Fuel: 1+20 to the destination and 0+35 to the alternate. She plans 1+20 plus 45 minutes. What is missing?
options: Nothing; the 45 minutes covers the alternate leg
A second 45-minute reserve for the alternate leg
The 35 minutes to the alternate, before the 45-minute reserve
Nothing; IFR only needs the 30-minute day reserve
steps.why: Fuel must cover the destination, then the alternate, then 45 minutes at normal cruising speed: 1+20 + 0+35 + 0+45 = 2+40 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(3)]].

steps.s: At 7 a.m. there is frost on the wings. She says the sun will take care of it while they taxi. What do you do?
options: Agree; frost blows off well before rotation
Accept it if it is thin enough to see the paint
Plan a faster rotation speed to make up for it
Have her remove all of it before flight
steps.why: Even very small amounts of frost can hurt the wing, so all of it comes off before flight [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(9)]]; never assume contamination will blow off [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-4b(4)]].
